course.title: Mobile App Development
course.description: A framework-neutral tour of how mobile apps are built — from the native vs cross-platform vs PWA choice, through screens and navigation, touch UI, state and data, and device features, to shipping on the app stores. Structure and learning outcomes draw on the ACM Computing Curricula recommendations for software development.

questions.prompt: A "native" mobile app is best described as one that is…
options: a web page saved to the home screen
built for one platform using that platform's own SDK
an app written only in JavaScript
questions.explanation: Native means built against a single platform's SDK — e.g. SwiftUI on iOS, Jetpack Compose on Android. Covered in 'How mobile apps run'.

questions.prompt: Cross-platform frameworks like React Native and Flutter mainly let you…
options: write separate code for each OS
share one codebase across iOS and Android
questions.explanation: One codebase targeting multiple platforms is the whole point — see 'How mobile apps run'.

questions.prompt: A Progressive Web App (PWA) runs…
options: in the browser engine, but can be installed and work offline
questions.explanation: A PWA is a website with a manifest and a service worker — installable and offline-capable. See 'How mobile apps run'.

questions.prompt: When a user switches away from your app, the OS usually moves it to the … state.
questions.explanation: Apps move foreground → background and may be suspended — see 'The app lifecycle'.

questions.prompt: For comfortable touch, a tappable control should be at least about…
questions.explanation: Both Apple and Google recommend roughly 44–48 px minimum touch targets — see 'Designing for touch'.

questions.prompt: To keep small data on the device between launches, you'd use…
options: on-device storage such as key-value or a local database
questions.explanation: Memory is cleared when the app closes; persistent local storage survives — see 'State and data'.

questions.prompt: Fetching fresh data from a server is normally done by…
options: making an HTTP request to a remote API
questions.explanation: Apps talk to backends over HTTP/HTTPS, usually returning JSON — see 'State and data'.

questions.prompt: Before an app reaches most users on iOS or Android, it typically must be…
options: code-signed and passed through store review
questions.explanation: Store apps are signed and reviewed against policy before release — see the applied project and key terms.

lessons.title: How mobile apps run: native, cross-platform, PWA
lessons.grammar_note: Native = one platform's own SDK; cross-platform = one codebase, many platforms; PWA = the web, installed.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain the three main ways to build a mobile app and choose sensibly between them. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, what makes an app 'native' rather than a saved web page?

sections.heading: The idea
Worked examples
sections.text: Say you're building a simple notes app. Native: fastest and most polished, but you write it twice (once per platform) and need two skill sets. Cross-platform: one team, one codebase, ~90% shared — a common default for startups in 2026. PWA: instantly shippable from a URL, great reach, but historically limited on iOS for things like background push. Reading the trade-off backwards: if your killer feature is a cutting-edge camera API, you lean native; if it's 'ship everywhere this quarter', you lean cross-platform or PWA.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Pick the best fit and say why: (1) a bank that needs the strongest security and platform biometrics; (2) a two-person startup shipping to iOS and Android next month; (3) a coupon page you want users to 'install' from a link with no store review; (4) a game needing maximum graphics performance. Answers: (1) native — deepest platform integration; (2) cross-platform — one codebase, two stores; (3) PWA — installable web, no store gate; (4) native — closest to the GPU.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking 'cross-platform' means 'write once, never touch platform code' — you still handle platform differences and store rules. Mistake: assuming a PWA is 'not a real app' — installed PWAs launch full-screen and run offline. Exit: (a) Which approach needs no app-store review to reach users? (b) Name the file that makes a PWA installable. Answers: (a) PWA; (b) the web app manifest.

lessons.title: The app lifecycle: screens and navigation
lessons.grammar_note: Lifecycle states: foreground ⇄ background → suspended. Never assume your app stayed running.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Describe the states an app moves through and how users move between screens. Warm-up: what state is your app usually in the moment a phone call interrupts it?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text:
The OS controls your app's *lifecycle*. An app is *foreground* (visible, interactive), *background* (not visible — a call, the home button, another app), or *suspended/terminated* (the OS reclaimed its memory). The rule: save important state when you leave the foreground, because you may never get a clean shutdown. Inside the app, users move between *screens* through a *navigator* that keeps a *stack* — pushing a new screen on top and popping back to return. Tabs, drawers, and modals are variations on the same idea. A minimal declarative route setup looks like:
```jsx
<Stack>
  <Screen name="Home" component={Home} />
  <Screen name="Details" component={Details} />
</Stack>
// navigate('Details', { id: 42 }) pushes; goBack() pops.
```
The id passed to `Details` is a *route parameter* — how one screen tells the next what to show.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: A shopping app: the product list is the bottom of the stack; tapping an item pushes a detail screen; tapping 'Reviews' pushes another; the back gesture pops them off one at a time. Lifecycle in action: the user backgrounds the app mid-checkout to copy a coupon; when they return, a well-built app restores the half-filled form because it saved that state on entering the background — not because the app 'stayed alive'.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Answer: (1) User taps 'Settings' from the home screen — push or pop? (2) User presses the system back gesture — push or pop? (3) A notification pulls the user away for 20 minutes — which lifecycle state? (4) Where should you save a draft the user is typing? Answers: (1) push; (2) pop; (3) background (possibly then suspended); (4) when moving to the background, into persistent storage.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming a screen you left is still mounted and holding data — it may have been popped or the app suspended. Mistake: doing heavy work in the foreground path so the first screen is slow to appear. Exit: (a) What data structure models forward/back navigation? (b) When is the safest moment to persist unsaved input? Answers: (a) a stack; (b) when the app enters the background.

lessons.title: Designing for touch: UI components and layout
lessons.grammar_note: Fingers aren't cursors: big targets, generous spacing, layouts that flex to any screen.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Assemble a screen from standard UI components and lay it out for touch on many screen sizes. Warm-up: roughly how big should a tap target be?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text:
Screens are built from a small vocabulary of *components*: text, images, buttons, text fields, lists, and switches. You compose them and let a *layout engine* — typically *flexbox* — position them, instead of hard-coding pixel positions, so the design adapts from a small phone to a tablet. Touch changes the rules: a finger is far less precise than a mouse pointer, so tap targets should be about *44–48 px* on a side with breathing room between them, and important actions belong within easy thumb reach. Long lists must be *virtualized* — only the visible rows are rendered — or scrolling stutters. A flex row that spaces two buttons apart:
```jsx
<View style={{ flexDirection: 'row', justifyContent: 'space-between', padding: 16 }}>
  <Button title="Cancel" />
  <Button title="Save" />
</View>
```
No absolute coordinates — the row re-flows on any width.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: A sign-in screen: a column with a logo, an email field, a password field, and a full-width 'Log in' button, each with padding so thumbs don't mis-tap. A contacts screen with 5,000 entries uses a virtualized list, so memory and scrolling stay flat whether there are 50 or 50,000 rows. Reversing the reasoning: if a QA report says 'buttons hard to hit on small phones', the fix is usually larger targets and more spacing, not a smaller font.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Decide the better choice: (1) two tiny 20 px icons touching vs 44 px icons with a gap; (2) rendering all 5,000 list rows at once vs virtualizing; (3) fixed pixel positions vs a flex layout for tablet support; (4) a primary action top-left vs within thumb reach. Answers: (1) 44 px with a gap; (2) virtualize; (3) flex layout; (4) within thumb reach.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: designing only for your own large phone and shipping targets that are unusable on small screens or for people with motor impairments. Mistake: rendering an entire long list eagerly. Exit: (a) Which layout system flexes across screen sizes? (b) Why virtualize a long list? Answers: (a) flexbox; (b) it renders only visible rows, keeping scrolling smooth and memory low.

questions.prompt: You need one codebase on both iOS and Android with near-native feel. Best fit?
questions.explanation: Cross-platform frameworks (React Native, Flutter) share one codebase across platforms.

questions.prompt: What makes a PWA installable to the home screen?
questions.explanation: The manifest declares name, icon, and display so the browser can install it.

questions.prompt: Navigating forward and back between screens is modeled by a…
questions.explanation: Push a new screen, pop to go back — last-in, first-out.

questions.prompt: The safest moment to persist unsaved user input is when the app…
questions.explanation: Backgrounding may be followed by suspension, so save state there.

questions.prompt: A comfortable minimum touch-target size is about…
questions.explanation: Platform guidelines converge near 44–48 px for reliable tapping.

questions.prompt: A list of 5,000 rows should be…
options: virtualized so only visible rows render
questions.explanation: Virtualization keeps scrolling smooth and memory bounded.

lessons.title: State and data: local storage and calling APIs
lessons.grammar_note: State lives in memory (gone on close); persistence lives on disk; fresh data comes from the network.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Distinguish in-memory state, on-device persistence, and remote data, and sketch how an app fetches from an API. Warm-up: if you store something in a plain variable, does it survive the app closing?

sections.heading: The idea
Worked examples
sections.text: A weather app: on open it reads the last-saved city from key-value storage (instant), shows cached readings from its local database (works offline), then fires an API request for the latest forecast and updates the screen when it returns. Split by lifetime: the currently-typed search term is state; the saved 'home city' is persistence; the live forecast is remote data. Design the offline story first and the app still feels usable on a train with no signal.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Classify each as in-memory state, on-device persistence, or remote data: (1) the text a user is typing right now; (2) their saved dark-mode preference; (3) today's currency exchange rates; (4) a cached list shown instantly on launch. Answers: (1) in-memory state; (2) on-device persistence; (3) remote data; (4) on-device persistence (a cache).

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming the network always succeeds — no loading or error state, so the app looks frozen or blank. Mistake: storing a large structured dataset in a key-value store instead of a local database. Exit: (a) Name the three UI states every network request needs. (b) Which storage suits a single small preference? Answers: (a) loading, success, error; (b) a key-value store.

lessons.title: Device features: camera, location, notifications
lessons.grammar_note: Powerful hardware is permission-gated: ask in context, degrade gracefully if denied.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain, at a concept level, how apps use the camera, location, and notifications behind the permission system. Warm-up: what should happen if a user says 'no' to a location prompt?

sections.heading: The idea
Worked examples
sections.text: A delivery app: it asks for location only after the user taps 'Track my order' (in context, so the prompt makes sense), uses coarse location for the map, and sends a push notification — routed through the OS push service — when the courier is near, even if the app is closed. A receipt scanner requests the camera the moment the user taps 'Scan', and if denied, offers manual entry instead of a dead end.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Answer: (1) Which notification type can arrive when the app is fully closed, from a server? (2) A map needs the city, not the exact street — request precise or coarse location? (3) When is the best moment to ask for camera access? (4) What should the app do if permission is denied? Answers: (1) push; (2) coarse; (3) right when the user triggers the camera feature; (4) degrade gracefully with a fallback and a way to enable it later.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: requesting every permission on first launch, before the user sees any value — most people decline. Mistake: treating a denied permission as fatal instead of offering an alternative. Exit: (a) What triggers a *push* notification versus a *local* one? (b) Name one way to raise the odds a user grants a permission. Answers: (a) push comes from a server via the OS push service, local is scheduled by the app itself; (b) ask in context, explaining the benefit at the point of use.

items.translation: an app built against one platform's own SDK for maximum performance and integration
items.example: The iOS team wrote the native app in Swift with SwiftUI.

items.translation: a toolkit like React Native or Flutter that runs one codebase on iOS and Android
items.example: They chose a cross-platform framework to ship both stores from one codebase.

items.translation: a website with a manifest and service worker that can be installed and work offline
items.example: The coupon page ships as a PWA, so there's no store review.

items.translation: the OS-controlled states an app moves through: foreground, background, suspended
items.example: Save the draft when the app lifecycle enters the background.

items.translation: on-device storage (key-value or a local database) that survives closing the app
items.example: The theme setting lives in persistent storage, not memory.

items.translation: the signing and policy check an app passes before release on the stores
items.example: The build cleared app-store review in two days.

questions.prompt: Data held only in a plain variable is lost when…
questions.explanation: In-memory state does not survive the app closing — use persistent storage.

questions.prompt: A single small preference like dark mode is best kept in…
questions.explanation: Key-value storage suits small, simple values.

questions.prompt: Every network request's UI should handle which set of states?
questions.explanation: Networks are slow and fail, so show loading, success, and error.

questions.prompt: A notification sent from a server that can reach a closed app is a…
questions.explanation: Push notifications travel through the OS push service from a backend.

questions.prompt: The best time to request camera permission is…
options: at first launch, before any value is shown
right when the user taps a scan/photo feature
questions.explanation: In-context requests, explained at point of use, get granted far more often.

questions.prompt: If a user denies a permission, a well-built app should…
questions.explanation: Offer an alternative path and a way to enable it later.

lessons.title: Applied project: design a simple app

sections.heading: The task
sections.text: Design (on paper — no code required) a small, single-purpose mobile app. Good candidates: a habit tracker, a tip splitter, a local-events finder, or a simple recipe box. You'll specify its screens, navigation, data, and one device feature, and justify your build approach.

sections.heading: Milestones
sections.text: 1) State the app's one job in a sentence. 2) List 3–4 screens and draw the navigation (which screen pushes to which). 3) Split your data into in-memory state, on-device persistence, and remote data, saying what lives where. 4) Choose exactly one device feature (camera, location, or notifications) and describe when you'd request its permission and what happens if it's denied. 5) Pick native, cross-platform, or PWA and give one reason. 6) Note one thing you'd check before app-store review (e.g. a privacy explanation for the permission you use).

sections.heading: Self-check rubric
sections.text: ✔ The app has a single, clear job. ✔ Navigation is drawn as a screen stack, not a vague list. ✔ Each piece of data is correctly placed as state, persistence, or remote — and offline behavior is addressed. ✔ The device feature requests permission in context and degrades gracefully on denial. ✔ The build-approach choice is justified in one honest trade-off. If all five hold, you've designed a mobile app the way a professional would scope one.
